Under the hood

How the formula engine works

Lattice isn't a styled table — it's a real calculation engine written from scratch in vanilla JavaScript. Type = in any cell and your text is tokenized, parsed into a syntax tree, and evaluated against a live dependency graph. Here's the whole pipeline.

1. The pipeline

Every formula travels the same path. Edit cell D5 to =B5-C5 and Lattice runs:

// 1 — tokenize: split the raw text into typed tokens "=B5-C5" → [ REF "B5", OP "-", REF "C5" ] // 2 — parse: recursive descent builds an AST { binary "-", left: ref B5, right: ref C5 } // 3 — extract deps: which cells does this read? deps = { B5, C5 } // registered in the dependency graph // 4 — evaluate against the sheet, with memoization + cycle guard result = value(B5) − value(C5)

2. Tokenizer

The tokenizer is a hand-written scanner. It recognises numbers (including 1.5e3 and a trailing %), quoted strings with escaped "", cell references (A1, $B$2), ranges via :, booleans, every operator, and function names (an identifier immediately followed by (). Anything else becomes a #NAME?.

3. Recursive-descent parser

A classic precedence-climbing recursive-descent parser turns tokens into a tree. Each grammar rule is one method, lowest precedence on the outside:

expr := compare compare := concat ( (= <> < > <= >=) concat )* concat := additive ( & additive )* additive := term ( (+ -) term )* term := power ( (* /) power )* power := unary ( ^ unary )* // right-associative unary := (+|-) unary | postfix postfix := primary ( % )* primary := NUMBER | STRING | BOOL | REF ( ":" REF )? // a cell or a range | NAME "(" args ")" // a function call | "(" expr ")"

Because precedence is encoded in the call chain, =2+3*4^2 correctly evaluates to 50 (power, then multiply, then add), and parentheses override it: =(2+3)*4 is 20.

4. Dependency graph & recalculation

When a formula compiles, Lattice records the set of cells it reads and adds reverse edges to a dependency graph. A recalculation walks every formula cell and resolves its value lazily and recursively: reading D14 (a SUM) pulls each cell in its range, which may themselves be formulas, all the way down. Results are memoised per pass so a cell is never computed twice.

Try it: in the budget template, change C6 (Groceries actual). The category difference D6, the % Used in E6, the SUM totals on row 14, the average, the max and the over-budget IF all update in a single pass.

5. Circular-reference detection

If A1 is =B1 and B1 is =A1, there's no valid value. Lattice detects this two ways: a recursion stack catches a cell that re-enters itself mid-evaluation, and a depth-first colouring pass over the dependency graph marks every cell on a cycle. Both surface as #CIRC! instead of hanging.

A1: =B1 + 1 B1: =A1 * 2 ↓ A1 → #CIRC! B1 → #CIRC! // the whole cycle is flagged

6. Worked examples

These all work in the editor right now — copy one into the formula bar:

FormulaWhat it doesResult*
=SUM(1,2,3,4)add a list of numbers10
=AVERAGE(10,20,30)mean, ignoring blanks & text20
=IF(5>3,"yes","no")branch on a comparisonyes
=ROUND(3.14159,2)round to 2 decimals3.14
=CONCAT("Q",1," report")join values into textQ1 report
=2+3*4^2operator precedence50
=COUNTIF(A1:A9,">100")count cells matching a rule(range)
=IF(AND(B2>0,C2>0),"ok","check")nested boolean logicok / check
=10/0handled error, not a crash#DIV/0!

*Numeric results assume the referenced cells are empty in a fresh sheet.

7. Full function reference

Lattice ships 50+ functions. Arithmetic + − * / ^, comparisons, string concat with &, percentages and absolute references ($A$1) are all built in too.
